lessons.title: Surface Preparation for Tropical and Arid Climates
lessons.body: Surface preparation is the foundation of every durable paint job, and in Africa the stakes are higher because substrates face intense sun, seasonal downpours, harmattan dust, salt air along the coast, and rapid temperature swings between day and night. A painter who skips or rushes preparation will watch a beautiful finish fail within one rainy season. This lesson gives you a practical, business-first system for preparing walls, wood, and metal so your work lasts and your reputation grows. Start with a proper assessment. Walk the site with the client and note the substrate type: cement block, rendered plaster, adobe, stone, timber, or metal. Check for dampness by pressing a dry cloth or plastic sheet against the wall for a few hours; if moisture appears, you must solve the water source before painting. In many African towns, rising damp from the ground and leaking roofs are the top causes of peeling paint. Explain to the client that painting over damp is money wasted, and offer a waterproofing or drainage fix as a separate paid service. Next, remove all loose material. Use a stiff wire brush, scraper, and sandpaper to take off flaking paint, chalky residue, and powdery plaster. On cement render, a common problem is efflorescence, the white salt deposit that appears when moisture moves through the wall. Brush it off dry, then wash with a mild acid solution or a proprietary efflorescence remover, rinse thoroughly, and let the wall dry completely. Never paint over efflorescence; it will push the new paint off. For dusty harmattan conditions, wipe surfaces with a damp cloth and allow to dry, because dust kills adhesion. Fill cracks and holes with a suitable filler. For interior plaster, use a fine filler; for exterior and structural cracks, use a sand-cement mortar or an epoxy patching compound. Undercut cracks slightly so the filler keys in, then smooth and sand flush. On timber, sand along the grain, fill nail holes, and treat knots with a knotting solution to stop resin bleeding. In coastal areas, timber needs extra protection because salt-laden air accelerates rot. On metal, remove rust by wire brushing or sanding to bare metal, then apply a rust-inhibiting primer within hours, especially in humid conditions. Priming is not optional. Use an alkali-resistant primer on new cement and plaster because fresh render is highly alkaline and will burn or blister ordinary paint. Use a wood primer on timber and a metal primer on steel. For previously painted surfaces, use a bonding primer if the old coating is sound but glossy. In hot, dry regions, prime early in the morning to avoid the paint drying too fast and losing penetration. In humid coastal regions, watch the dew point; if the surface is colder than the air, condensation will ruin the primer. Temperature and humidity control are practical skills. Most paints need surface temperatures between 10 and 35 degrees Celsius and relative humidity below 85 percent. In the Sahel, avoid painting in the afternoon when surfaces can exceed 50 degrees Celsius; the paint will skin over and crack. In the rainforest belt, paint when the wall is dry and rain is not expected for at least 24 hours. Buy a cheap moisture meter and a thermometer; these small tools win client trust and prevent costly rework. Safety and site management matter for your business. Wear dust masks when sanding, especially in old buildings where lead paint may be present. Use eye protection when mixing acids or caustic washes. Keep the site clean, cover floors and furniture, and dispose of debris responsibly. A tidy site signals professionalism and often leads to referrals. Finally, document your preparation. Take before photos, note the products used, and give the client a simple written scope. This protects you if problems arise and shows the value of the unseen work. Preparation can take 60 to 70 percent of total labour time, so price it properly. Many young painters underquote because they only count the visible coats. Build a checklist and a standard rate for preparation per square metre. When you explain why preparation costs what it does, clients understand and respect the price. Remember, in Africa word of mouth travels fast. A finish that survives three rainy seasons and a harmattan will bring you more work than any advertisement. Treat preparation as your competitive advantage, not a chore.

lessons.title: Choosing Paints, Primers, and Thinners for African Conditions
lessons.body: Choosing the right paint system is a business decision as much as a technical one. The wrong product means callbacks, refunds, and lost reputation. This lesson helps you match paints, primers, and thinners to African climates and budgets so you deliver value and protect your margin. Begin with the substrate and the exposure. Interior walls in a dry, dusty region need a washable, scrub-resistant finish because dust and smoke settle and clients wipe walls often. Exterior walls in high-rainfall areas need elastomeric or acrylic coatings that bridge hairline cracks and resist water. Coastal buildings need salt-resistant coatings and corrosion-resistant primers on metal. Hot inland areas need heat-reflective or light-coloured paints to reduce thermal stress and cooling costs. Understand the main paint types. Emulsion paints are water-based and come as matt, silk, or sheen. Matt emulsion hides imperfections but is less washable; silk and sheen are more durable and easier to clean, making them good for corridors, kitchens, and clinics. Gloss and satin enamels are solvent-based or water-based and form a hard, washable film; they suit woodwork, doors, and metal. Textured coatings hide poor plaster and are popular for exterior walls, but they trap dust in dry areas, so advise clients accordingly. Distemper and whitewash are cheap but short-lived; use them only for temporary or low-budget utility spaces and say so honestly. Primers are the bridge between substrate and topcoat. Alkali-resistant primer for new cement and plaster. Wood primer for timber, with aluminium primer for resinous woods. Zinc-rich or red oxide primer for steel. Etch primer for galvanised metal and aluminium. For previously painted surfaces, a bonding primer or a coat of the same type of paint thinned slightly can work, but test a small area first. Never mix incompatible systems; for example, do not put solvent-based paint over a water-based primer unless the primer is fully cured and the product data sheet allows it. Thinners and solvents must match the paint. Water-based paints clean up with water, but some need a small amount of water to thin, never more than the manufacturer states. Solvent-based paints use white spirit, turpentine, or proprietary thinners. Using the wrong thinner causes orange peel, poor flow, or complete failure. In hot weather, a slow-evaporating thinner helps the paint flow and level; in humid weather, a faster thinner can reduce blushing. Always read the data sheet and keep a copy on your phone or in your van. Quantity estimation protects your profit. Measure the area and calculate square metres. One litre of emulsion covers roughly 10 to 14 square metres per coat on smooth surfaces, less on rough or porous walls. Two topcoats are standard for a durable finish; some colours, especially reds, yellows, and deep blues, need three. Primer coverage is often 8 to 12 square metres per litre. Add 10 percent waste for spillage, touch-ups, and texture. Present the estimate in writing with the number of coats, brands, and finish. Clients appreciate transparency and are less likely to haggle when they see the logic. Colour selection is a commercial skill. In hot climates, light colours reflect heat and make rooms feel cooler; dark colours absorb heat and can cause thermal movement and premature failure on exterior walls. In dusty areas, mid-tones and earth tones hide dust better than pure white. In coastal towns, light blues and greens are culturally popular and practical. Use colour cards, and where possible, apply a small sample patch for the client to see in natural light. Charge for sample patches if they are extensive, or include one or two free as a sales tool. Health and environmental considerations are increasingly important. Low-VOC and lead-free paints are safer for workers and families, especially in schools and clinics. Many African countries are phasing out lead in paint, so choose reputable brands with clear labels. Water-based paints are easier to clean up and less flammable, which reduces site risk. Store paints away from direct sun, keep lids sealed, and never pour leftovers down drains. For your business, build relationships with two or three reliable suppliers. Ask for trade discounts, technical data sheets, and training. Keep a simple stock record so you do not run out mid-job. When a client insists on a cheap product that you know will fail, put your advice in writing and offer a warranty only on your labour, not the material. This protects you and educates the client. Finally, review every job. Note which products performed well and which failed. Over time you will build a personal product guide for your region, and that knowledge is worth more than any certificate.

lessons.title: Application Techniques: Brushes, Rollers, and Spray in the Field
lessons.body: Good application turns preparation and quality materials into a professional finish. This lesson covers brushes, rollers, and spray equipment with practical field methods for African conditions, plus the business habits that keep you fast, clean, and profitable. Start with brushes. A good brush holds its shape, releases paint evenly, and cleans well. For water-based paints, use synthetic filaments; for solvent-based paints, use natural bristle or a synthetic blend that resists solvents. Keep different brushes for different tasks: a 50mm cutting brush for edges, a 75mm to 100mm brush for large flat areas, and a small sash brush for windows and trim. Break in a new brush by wetting it with the appropriate thinner, working it against a hard surface, and combing it straight. After use, clean water-based paint with warm soapy water and solvent-based paint with white spirit, then shape the bristles and hang or store flat. A well-kept brush lasts years and saves money. Rollers speed up large areas. Choose the nap length for the surface: short nap for smooth plaster, medium for light texture, long nap for rough exterior render. Use a roller frame with a comfortable handle and a tray with a grid. Load the roller evenly, roll in a W pattern, then finish with light parallel strokes in one direction for a uniform finish. Do not over-roll; it dries the paint and leaves marks. For ceilings, use an extension pole to avoid ladders and reduce fatigue. In hot weather, work in smaller sections so the paint does not dry before you finish blending. Spray application is fast and gives a smooth finish, ideal for large walls, fences, and metalwork. There are three main types: airless, conventional compressed air, and high-volume low-pressure. Airless sprayers are efficient for big jobs but need careful masking and a steady hand. Conventional spray gives fine control for furniture and trim. High-volume low-pressure is popular for site work because it reduces overspray. Thinning must follow the manufacturer data sheet; too thick clogs the gun, too thin causes runs. Keep the gun perpendicular to the surface, about 20 to 30 centimetres away, and overlap each pass by 50 percent. Move at a steady speed. Spray in calm conditions; wind carries overspray onto cars, laundry, and neighbours, which can cost you money and goodwill. Mask windows, doors, floors, and fittings with tape and plastic sheeting. In dusty harmattan conditions, spray early morning when air is still and dust is low. In humid coastal areas, watch for blushing on solvent-based finishes; a retarder thinner can help. Cutting in is the mark of a craftsman. Use a steady hand and a quality cutting brush to paint a straight line where wall meets ceiling, skirting, or trim. If you are not confident, use masking tape, but remove it while the paint is still slightly wet to avoid peeling the film. For stripes and patterns, measure and mark with chalk or pencil, then tape carefully. Decorative techniques such as sponging, ragging, and stencilling can add value for clients who want something special. Practise on boards first, and price these as premium services. Weather and timing affect application. Paint the shady side of the building first; it stays workable longer. Avoid painting in direct sun on hot days because the surface is too hot and the paint dries too fast. In rainy season, watch the sky and stop early enough to allow at least two hours of drying before any rain. Keep a tarpaulin or plastic sheet to cover work if rain threatens. For exterior work, plan around the forecast and communicate delays to the client. Site discipline keeps you efficient. Set up your area with everything you need: paint, brushes, rollers, trays, rags, masking tape, and a rubbish bag. Work from top to bottom and from one corner to the exit so you do not walk through wet paint. Clean as you go. At the end of each day, seal paint tins, clean tools, and secure the site. A clean site reduces accidents and impresses clients. Pricing application is about time and skill. Estimate square metres per hour for each method: brushing is slowest, rolling is medium, spraying is fastest but needs more preparation and masking. Add time for cutting in, masking, and cleanup. Charge more for intricate work, high ceilings, and occupied spaces. Offer a written quote with a clear scope. Finally, train your team. Show them the correct technique, check their work, and give feedback. A crew that applies paint properly uses less material, finishes faster, and produces fewer callbacks. That is how you grow from a one-person operation into a trusted painting business.

lessons.title: Curing, Drying, and Protecting Finishes in Harsh Weather
lessons.body: A paint job is not finished when the last brushstroke lands. Curing, drying, and protection determine whether the finish lasts one season or many. In Africa, intense sun, high humidity, rain, dust, and temperature swings all attack fresh paint. This lesson teaches you how to manage those forces and turn durability into a selling point. First, understand the difference between drying and curing. Drying is when the paint loses solvent or water and feels dry to touch. Curing is the chemical cross-linking that gives the film its final hardness, adhesion, and resistance. Water-based paints dry quickly but cure over days or weeks. Solvent-based and two-pack paints cure more slowly and are more sensitive to temperature and humidity. In cool, humid highland areas, curing can take much longer than the label suggests. In hot, dry areas, the surface may dry too fast, trapping solvent and causing cracks or poor adhesion. Manage the environment. Aim for the manufacturer recommended temperature and humidity range. If the surface is too hot, wait until late afternoon or early morning. If humidity is too high, use dehumidifiers in enclosed spaces or postpone exterior work. Good ventilation helps solvent-based paints cure and reduces health risks, but avoid strong drafts that carry dust onto wet surfaces. In harmattan season, dust is the enemy. Close windows where possible, use temporary plastic screens, and choose a calm time of day. If dust settles on a tacky surface, do not try to wipe it off; let it dry, sand lightly, and recoat. Protect fresh paint from rain. Water-based paints need at least two to four hours of dry weather before light rain, and longer for full resistance. Solvent-based paints can be damaged by rain even after they feel dry. Keep tarpaulins, plastic sheets, and battens on site. If rain is forecast, plan to stop early enough to cover the work. Never paint exterior surfaces when rain is imminent, and never paint a wall that is still damp from previous rain. Sun exposure is a major factor. Ultraviolet light breaks down binders and fades pigments, especially on south and west facing walls in the southern hemisphere and north and west facing walls in the northern hemisphere. Use UV-resistant exterior paints and consider light colours that reflect heat. On metal roofs and walls, thermal movement can crack rigid coatings; use flexible or elastomeric products. On timber, maintain a protective oil or varnish coat every year or two, especially in coastal and high-rainfall areas. Temperature swings cause expansion and contraction. In desert regions, day and night temperatures can differ by 20 degrees Celsius or more. This stress opens hairline cracks and lets water in. Elastomeric coatings bridge these cracks and are worth the extra cost. On joints and seams, use flexible sealants rather than rigid fillers. Inspect after the first hot and cold cycle and touch up any failures. Maintenance is a business opportunity. Offer clients a maintenance plan: an annual inspection, cleaning, and touch-up service. This creates recurring income and keeps your work looking good, which generates referrals. Teach clients simple care: wash walls with mild soap and water, avoid abrasive cleaners, fix leaks promptly, and trim vegetation away from walls. Provide a simple care sheet with your contact details. Warranty and documentation protect you. Give a written warranty that states what is covered, for how long, and what voids it, such as structural movement, leaks, or misuse. Keep records of products, batch numbers, application dates, and weather conditions. If a problem appears, you can diagnose whether it is a product fault, a substrate issue, or a maintenance failure. This evidence helps you resolve disputes fairly and protects your reputation. Troubleshooting common failures is a core skill. Blistering usually means moisture behind the film; find and fix the water source, then remove blistered paint and repaint. Peeling often means poor preparation or incompatible coatings; strip back and start again. Chalking is normal weathering of some exterior paints, but excessive chalking means the binder has failed; clean and recoat with a quality exterior product. Mould and mildew appear in humid areas; clean with a fungicidal wash, fix damp, and use a mould-resistant paint. Yellowing of alkyd enamels in dark rooms is common; use water-based alternatives where possible. Fading is caused by UV and pigment quality; choose lightfast colours for exteriors. Each failure is a lesson. Record it, share it with your team, and adjust your methods. Finally, think about the client experience. A clean, well-protected finish that survives the first rainy season builds trust. Follow up after three months and after one year. A short message or visit shows you stand behind your work. In many African markets, trust and personal relationships drive repeat business more than price. By mastering curing, drying, and protection, you turn a one-time job into a long-term relationship and a steady stream of referrals.

lessons.title: Pricing, Quoting, and Running a Profitable Painting Business
lessons.body: Technical skill alone will not keep your painting business alive. You must price correctly, quote professionally, manage cash, and market your services. This lesson gives you a practical business framework for the African market, where competition is fierce, clients bargain hard, and material costs can change quickly. Start with accurate measurement. Break the job into surfaces: walls, ceilings, trim, doors, windows, metalwork, and any special features. Measure length times height for each area and subtract large openings. Record everything in a notebook or phone app. For exterior work, include gables, parapets, and hard-to-reach areas. For interiors, note ceiling height and whether furniture must be moved. Measurement is the basis of a fair price and prevents disputes. Next, calculate costs. There are four main categories: materials, labour, overhead, and profit. Materials include paint, primer, filler, sandpaper, tape, plastic sheeting, thinner, and cleaning supplies. Get current prices from your supplier and add 10 percent for waste and price changes. Labour is your time and your team time. Decide a fair daily or hourly rate based on local market conditions, skill level, and the risk of the job. Do not forget preparation time, which is often the largest labour component. Overhead includes transport, phone data, tools replacement, insurance, taxes, and storage. Many small painters ignore overhead and then wonder why they are always broke. Add a realistic percentage, often 10 to 20 percent. Profit is not a luxury; it is what lets you reinvest, survive slow months, and grow. Add 15 to 30 percent profit depending on the market and the job complexity. Present the quote clearly. Use a written quote with your business name, client name, date, site address, and a detailed scope. List the surfaces, the number of coats, the products and brands, the preparation work, and the timeline. State what is not included, such as major repairs, waterproofing, or furniture moving. Give a total price and payment terms. A common and fair structure is a deposit of 40 to 50 percent to buy materials, a progress payment of 30 percent when the work is half done, and the balance on completion. For larger jobs, agree on weekly or milestone payments. Always get a signed acceptance before starting. This protects both sides and makes the client serious. Handle bargaining professionally. Do not drop your price without reducing scope. If the client wants a lower price, offer fewer coats, a cheaper paint line, or exclude certain areas. Explain the trade-off honestly. Never promise a premium finish at a budget price. A client who respects your expertise will pay fairly. If a client refuses a fair price, walk away politely; a loss-making job is worse than no job. Manage cash flow carefully. Keep business money separate from personal money. Track every expense and payment. Use a simple ledger or a phone spreadsheet. Save a portion of each payment for taxes, tools, and slow periods. Buy materials in bulk when you have a secure job and storage, but do not tie up all your cash in stock. Build relationships with suppliers for credit terms if possible, but pay on time to keep your reputation. Market your business consistently. Word of mouth is powerful, so ask satisfied clients for referrals and testimonials. Keep a portfolio of before and after photos, especially of challenging jobs. Use social media and messaging apps to share your work with local groups. Print simple business cards and a flyer with your services, service area, and phone number. Offer a referral discount to clients who bring you new business. Partner with real estate agents, landlords, builders, and interior designers who need reliable painters. Train and manage your team. Hire workers with a good attitude and teach them your standards. Pay fairly and on time. Use a simple contract that states duties, hours, pay, and safety rules. Provide basic safety equipment such as masks, gloves, and eye protection. Motivate your team with bonuses for quality and speed, but never sacrifice safety or workmanship for speed. A stable team lets you take on bigger jobs and earn more. Plan for growth. Set monthly and annual income goals. Review your jobs to see which types are most profitable. Maybe exterior work pays better than interiors, or commercial contracts beat residential. Invest in better tools, a vehicle, and training. Keep learning about new products and techniques. Join or form a painters association to share knowledge and negotiate better prices. Finally, protect your health and your future. Painting can expose you to dust, solvents, and heavy lifting. Use safety gear, take breaks, and drink water in hot weather. Save for retirement and emergencies. Insurance for tools and public liability is worth considering as you grow. A professional painting business in Africa can support a family, create jobs, and build beautiful spaces. With disciplined pricing, clear quoting, and smart management, you turn your craft into a lasting enterprise.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Estimating, Mixing, and Applying Paint on African Sites

This reference lesson consolidates the numbers, ratios, and field checks that separate a profitable painting job from a loss-making one. In African markets, where paint can be 30â50% of a job's direct cost and transport to remote sites is expensive, getting quantities and mixing right the first time is the difference between a 15% margin and a 15% loss. Use this as your site bible alongside Module 5's other lessons.

All figures here assume standard trade practice: 2 coats on previously painted sound surfaces, 3 coats on bare or porous substrates, and coverage rates verified against manufacturer data sheets. Where local brands differ, always defer to the product data sheet â but use these benchmarks to sanity-check quotes and avoid under-ordering.

Table 1: Coverage Rates and Consumption Benchmarks for Common African Market Paints

These figures reflect typical coverage on smooth, primed masonry and plaster â the dominant substrate in African residential and commercial work. Porous or rough surfaces can reduce coverage by 20â40%. Always add a 10% wastage allowance for brush/roller loss, spillage, and touch-ups.

Paint Type Typical Coverage (mÂ²/L/coat) Recommended Coats Drying Time (touch / recoat) Thinner Ratio Typical 20 L Price (USD equiv.)
Emulsion (vinyl/acrylic), interior 8â10 2 1 h / 4 h Water 5â10% 45â75
Emulsion, exterior weather-resistant 6â8 2â3 1 h / 4â6 h Water 5% 70â120
Gloss enamel (oil-based) 10â12 2 4 h / 16 h White spirit 5â10% 80â140
Masonry/textured coating 3â5 2 2 h / 6 h Water 5% 60â110
Primer (alkali-resisting) 8â10 1 2 h / 4 h Water 10% 35â60
Wood primer (solvent) 10â12 1 4 h / 12 h White spirit 10% 50â90

Sources: Coverage ranges compiled from Crown Paints Kenya, Plascon (South Africa), and Dulux/AkzoNobel product data sheets; price bands from Nairobi, Lagos, and Accra trade surveys 2023â2024. Drying times assume 25â30Â°C and 50â70% RH. In arid conditions (RH <30%, >35Â°C), reduce recoat times by 30â40% but watch for flash drying and brush drag.

Table 2: Labour Productivity and Costing Benchmarks for African Painting Crews

Labour is typically 40â55% of a painting contract price in Africa. These productivity rates assume a trained painter with basic scaffolding, working 8 hours with normal breaks. Unskilled helpers doing prep work are roughly 2.5Ã slower on surface preparation tasks.

Task Output per Painter-Day Unit Typical Day Rate (USD equiv.) Notes
Surface prep â sanding, filling, dusting 25â35 mÂ² 8â20 Helper can do 10â15 mÂ²/day
Emulsion â 2 coats, brush/roller 60â80 mÂ² 10â25 Spray: 150â200 mÂ²/day
Gloss enamel â 2 coats, trim/doors 20â30 mÂ² 12â28 Detailed work, slower
Exterior masonry â 2 coats 40â55 mÂ² 10â25 Add 20% for scaffolding
Priming â 1 coat 80â100 mÂ² 8â18 Fastest stage
Spray application â all coats 150â250 mÂ² 15â35 Requires masking + 15â25% paint waste

Sources: Productivity ranges adapted from ILO construction sector productivity studies and ILRI livestock-facility maintenance costing notes (relevant for agribusiness structures); day rates from Kenya National Bureau of Statistics, Nigeria NBS, and Ghana Statistical Service informal construction wage data 2023â2024, converted at prevailing rates.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CHEMICAL AND HEALTH HAZARDS

Solvent-based paints, thinners, and lead-containing old coatings are hazardous. In African field conditions, heat and poor ventilation dramatically increase risk.

  • Lead: Older paints (pre-1990s) in many African markets may contain lead. Sanding lead paint releases toxic dust â test before disturbing; use wet sanding and respirators.
  • Solvents: White spirit and xylene cause dizziness, headaches, and long-term organ damage. Work outdoors or with forced ventilation; never in sealed rooms without extraction.
  • Skin: Prolonged contact causes dermatitis. Wear nitrile gloves for solvent paints, latex for water-based.
  • Eyes: Splashes are common with spraying. Safety glasses or goggles mandatory.
  • Heat stress: Combine paint fumes with 35Â°C+ heat and you risk collapse. Rotate crew, hydrate every 20 minutes, schedule heavy work for early morning.
  • Disposal: Never pour thinners or paint residue down drains or onto soil â it contaminates water sources. Collect in sealed containers and dispose via licensed waste handlers.

Reference: WHO "Lead in Paint" fact sheet and ILO Chemical Safety in the Workplace guidance.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Measure net area, not gross. Deduct all doors, windows, and openings >0.5 mÂ². Add 10% wastage. Recheck before ordering.
  2. Verify substrate moisture. New plaster must cure 4â6 weeks in humid tropics, 2â3 weeks in arid zones. Test with a moisture meter â <16% for emulsion, <12% for solvent paints.
  3. Prime everything bare. Never skip primer on new plaster, wood, or metal. Alkali-resisting primer for masonry; wood primer for timber; zinc-rich or red oxide for steel.
  4. Mix to data sheet ratio, not guesswork. Over-thinning ruins durability and coverage. Use a measuring jug, not a "splash."
  5. Check weather windows. Don't apply exterior paint if rain is forecast within 4 hours (emulsion) or 8 hours (solvent). In arid zones, avoid applying in direct afternoon sun â surface temperature can exceed 50Â°C and cause blistering.
  6. Calculate litres per coat, then multiply. Formula: Litres = Net area Ã· Coverage rate Ã Number of coats. Round up to the nearest tin size.
  7. Price with a 15% contingency. African supply chains are unpredictable â a missing colourant or delayed delivery can stall a crew. Buffer the quote.
  8. Document before/after with photos. Essential for client disputes and for building your portfolio for the next tender.

Further Reading

  • WHO â Lead Poisoning and Health Fact Sheet (free, authoritative on lead paint hazards)
  • ILO â Chemical Safety in the Workplace (free guidance on solvent handling and PPE)
  • FAO â Simple Methods for Rural Construction and Finishing (free, covers low-cost building finishes relevant to African rural projects)
  • UN-Habitat â Housing and Construction Resources (free publications on affordable housing finishes)
  • ILO Publications â Construction Sector Productivity and Wages (free access to labour costing data)

Business-first note: Every number in this reference exists to protect your margin. Under-ordering paint means a second trip to town â often 2â4 hours and fuel you didn't quote. Over-ordering ties up cash. Measure twice, order once, and always carry the 10% wastage and 15% contingency. That is how painting businesses in Nairobi, Lagos, and Accra survive their second year.

quiz.q: Which type of paint is most suitable for a high-traffic hallway wall that needs to be scrubbable?
quiz.explanation: Silk emulsion forms a durable, wipeable film that withstands repeated cleaning, making it ideal for high-traffic areas.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of applying a primer before painting bare wood?
options: B) To seal the surface and improve adhesion
quiz.explanation: Primer seals porous bare wood and creates a key for the topcoat, improving adhesion and finish.

quiz.q: Which abrasive grade is typically used for final sanding between coats of paint?
quiz.explanation: Fine 240 grit removes nibs and flattens the surface without scratching through the fresh paint film.

quiz.q: When cutting in a ceiling line with emulsion, which tool gives the most control?
options: C) A 2 inch angled sash brush
quiz.explanation: A 2 inch angled sash brush allows precise control along the ceiling line and reduces the need for masking tape.

quiz.q: What does the term opacity refer to in a paint product?
options: A) The ability of the paint to hide the surface beneath
B) The speed at which the paint dries
C) The level of sheen on the finish
D) The resistance of the paint to mould
quiz.explanation: Opacity describes how well a paint obliterates or hides the colour and pattern of the substrate.

quiz.q: Which condition is most likely to cause blistering in a newly applied gloss finish?
options: A) Applying in a well-ventilated room
B) Painting over a damp or contaminated surface
quiz.explanation: Moisture or contamination under the paint film turns to vapour and lifts the coating, causing blisters.

quiz.q: What is the correct order for preparing a previously glossed door for repainting?
quiz.explanation: Degreasing removes grease, sanding provides a key, and undercoat prepares the surface for the topcoat.

quiz.q: Which safety precaution is essential when using solvent-based paint in an enclosed room?
options: D) Ensuring adequate ventilation and wearing a respirator
quiz.explanation: Solvent vapours are harmful, so good ventilation and a suitable respirator protect the painter from inhalation risks.

quiz.q: In hot arid regions of Africa, why should painting be avoided during the hottest part of the day?
options: B) Paint dries too fast causing lap marks and poor adhesion
quiz.explanation: Extreme heat accelerates drying, leading to lap marks and weak bonding.

quiz.q: Which surface preparation step is most critical before painting exterior walls in humid tropical Africa?
options: A) Sanding to a mirror finish
B) Removing all moisture and treating mould or algae
C) Applying a thick coat of varnish
quiz.explanation: Humidity encourages mould and algae, which must be removed for paint to adhere.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to apply exterior paint in a hot dry African climate?
options: A) Midday when surfaces are hottest
B) Early morning or late afternoon when temperatures are moderate
D) Just before a dust storm
quiz.explanation: Cooler times reduce flash drying and allow proper levelling.

quiz.q: Which primer is most suitable for bare metal surfaces in coastal African areas with salt air?
quiz.explanation: Anti-corrosive primers protect metal from salt-induced rust.

quiz.q: Why is it important to check the moisture content of masonry before painting in tropical Africa?
options: B) Excess moisture causes blistering and peeling
quiz.explanation: Trapped moisture pushes paint off the wall, causing blisters and peeling.

quiz.q: Which thinner is commonly used with oil-based paints in African conditions?
quiz.explanation: White spirit or turpentine is the standard thinner for oil-based paints.

quiz.q: What should you do if a surface in an arid region is too hot to touch before painting?
options: B) Wait until it cools or shade the surface
C) Add more thinner to the paint
D) Use a roller with long nap
quiz.explanation: Hot surfaces cause paint to dry too fast and fail to bond.

quiz.q: Which brush type is best for applying solvent-based paint on rough African masonry?
options: B) Stiff natural or synthetic bristle brush
quiz.explanation: Stiff bristles work paint into rough textures effectively.

quiz.q: In tropical humidity, what additive can help paint dry faster?
quiz.explanation: Driers accelerate curing when humidity slows drying.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of using a roller over a brush for large walls in African field work?
options: B) Faster coverage on large flat surfaces
quiz.explanation: Rollers cover large areas much faster than brushes.

quiz.q: Which safety gear is essential when spray painting in an African field environment?
quiz.explanation: Spray painting releases fumes and particles requiring respiratory and skin protection.

quiz.q: Why should paint not be applied in direct hot sun in arid Africa?
options: B) It causes rapid drying, blistering, and poor finish
C) It makes paint last longer
quiz.explanation: Direct sun dries paint too quickly, ruining the finish.

quiz.q: What is the recommended method to protect freshly painted exterior surfaces in harsh weather?
options: B) Use temporary shade or windbreaks during curing
quiz.explanation: Shade and windbreaks prevent rapid drying and contamination during curing.

quiz.q: Which factor most affects paint curing time in African climates?
quiz.explanation: Environmental conditions directly control how fast paint cures.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when quoting painting jobs in Africa?
options: B) Underestimating surface preparation and material wastage
quiz.explanation: Underestimating prep and wastage leads to loss of profit.

quiz.q: Which cost should always be included in a painting quote?
options: B) Labour, materials, transport, and contingency
quiz.explanation: A complete quote covers all direct and indirect costs.

quiz.q: Why is it important to measure surface area accurately when quoting?
options: B) To calculate correct paint quantity and cost
quiz.explanation: Accurate measurement prevents over- or under-ordering materials.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for pricing in competitive African markets?
options: B) Offer clear value and itemised pricing
quiz.explanation: Transparent itemised pricing builds trust and justifies value.

quiz.q: Which payment term is safest for a painting contractor in Africa?
options: A) Full payment after one year
B) Deposit before start and balance on completion
D) Payment only if client is happy
quiz.explanation: A deposit covers initial costs and reduces risk of non-payment.

quiz.q: What should be done if rain is expected during exterior painting in tropical Africa?
options: B) Stop and cover work until weather clears
quiz.explanation: Rain ruins fresh paint and must be avoided or protected against.

quiz.q: Which reference tool helps painters estimate paint quantity accurately?
options: B) Coverage rate on paint container and surface area calculation
quiz.explanation: Coverage rate plus area gives accurate paint quantity.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important for a painting business in Africa?
options: B) To track costs, profits, and improve future quotes
quiz.explanation: Records reveal true costs and guide better pricing decisions.
